extracted.intended_audience: readers interested in calendar computation and history (clergy, historians, astronomers, and calendar enthusiasts)
extracted.subtask_description: Procedures and supporting tables for finding Easter Day in any year under the Gregorian (new style) and Antegregorian/Julian (old style) calendars, including computation of dominical letter, golden number, epact, and final March/April day. Also guidance on using epact/new-and-full-moon tables and interpreting +/− day annotations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rule for determining Easter Day of the Gregorian Calendar
rubrics_metrics.description: A stepwise algorithm (numbered I–XV) to compute Easter in any given year of the new style (Gregorian) by computing I. year+1; II. quotient of year/4; III. centurial figures minus 16; IV. quotient of III/4; V. sum I+II+IV minus III; VI. remainder of V mod 7; VII. dominical letter = 7−VI (map 1..7 to A..G); VIII. golden number = remainder of (I divided by 19) (use 19 if no remainder); IX. quotient of (centurial figures − 17)/25; X. quotient of (centurial figures − IX − 15)/3; XI. remainder of (VIII + 10×(previous less number)) mod 30; XII. epact = XI + X + IV − III with thirties thrown out and special adjustments (see guidance); then depending on whether the epact is ≤23 or >23 compute XIII, XIV and finally XV to get the day in March or April on which Easter Sunday falls.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Full procedural notes and numerical examples are provided (example year 1849). Specific handling for the epact in step XII: if XII gives 24 change it into 25; if 25 change it into 26 whenever the golden number is greater than 11; if 0 change it into 30. When the Epact is 23 or less: XIII = 45 − epact; XIV = remainder of (27 − epact) mod 7 (use 7 if no remainder). When the Epact is greater than 23: XIII = 75 − epact; XIV = remainder of (57 − epact) mod 7 (use 7 if no remainder). XV: To XIII add VII (the dominical number), and add 7 more if XIV > VII, then subtract XIV; the result is the day of March (if >31 subtract 31 to get April). The page includes a worked table of intermediate values and final Easter days for many sample years to illustrate each step.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rule for determining Easter Day of the Antegregorian (old style) Calendar
rubrics_metrics.description: A corresponding numbered procedure (steps aligned with Gregorian numbering) to find Easter in any year of the old style (Julian), beginning with I. set down the given year; II. quotient of year/4; V. take 4 more than (I+II); VI. remainder of V mod 7; VII. dominical letter = 7−VI (map 1..7 to A..G); VIII. golden number = remainder of ((year+1)/19) (or 19 if no remainder); XII. epact = remainder of (11×VIII − 3) divided by 30 (or 30 if no remainder); then proceed with the epact-dependent XIII–XV to obtain the March/April day for Easter (old style).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The page gives the full numbered steps with an example for year 1287 and notes that the Antegregorian steps show what augmentations the Gregorian rule requires. For epact (step XII) compute remainder of (11×golden_number − 3) mod 30 (use 30 if no remainder). Then follow the same branching as in the Gregorian rule: when epact ≤23 compute XIII = 45 − epact and XIV = remainder of (27 − epact) mod 7 (use 7 if no remainder); when epact >23 use XIII = 75 − epact and XIV = remainder of (57 − epact) mod 7 (use 7 if no remainder). Finally use XV as in Gregorian to derive the calendar day (example yields Easter Day April 6 old style).

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of the epact/new-and-full-moon tables to find calendar new and full moons
rubrics_metrics.description: Given the epact for a year, locate that epact in the first or last column of the first table; in the same line the table shows the calendar days of the new and full moons for each month. The page supplies a large table of new and full moon days indexed by epact (for months Jan–Dec).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The table is generally correct but in a minority of cases may be off by one day; such errors are almost always a fraction of a day much less than twelve hours. The table uses '+' to indicate the truth is the day after the listed date and '−' to indicate the day before. Example: for epact 25 in 1867 the table shows New and Full moon dates with +/− annotations; the new moon of March is actually on the 6th (table shows 5+), full moon of April is on the 18th (table shows 18).

rubrics_metrics.name: Epact table coverage and continuation guidance
rubrics_metrics.description: A published epact table (listed for years 1850–1999) gives the epact for each year; the table may be extended from liturgical sources if needed beyond 1999.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The page notes that the epact table goes from 1850 to 1999 and that, should churches and liturgical practice remain, the epact table may be continued from their liturgy-books. It also explains how to read the epact table (take the epact of the required year and find the corresponding line in the new/full-moon table) and cautions about occasional one-day discrepancies (see plus/minus annotation guidance).
